books.title: Talk Like TED
books.author: Carmine Gallo
books.dek: The 9 public-speaking secrets of the world's top minds. Your notes, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: Unleash the Master Within
summary: Passion beats expertise. Viewers can tell if you care, and they're not stupid.
Your passion isn't skincare. It's helping young guys improve their lives while entertaining them.
Passion spreads: positive, charismatic people lift and persuade others. Hire for it.

sections.title: Be passionate
sections.md:
If you're not passionate about the thing you're speaking about, how is the audience going to care? It's not about being an expert as much as it is about being passionate about it, and **showing** that you're passionate. The viewers can tell. They're not stupid.

==It's not really about being passionate about the product.== It's not about being passionate about skincare, but about helping young people improve their lives while entertaining them.

sections.title: What makes your heart sing?
sections.md:
Ask yourself that question. It's a stronger version of "what are you passionate about?"

::: key
**What makes my heart sing?**
Helping people improve the way they feel about themselves, so they can be themselves, express themselves however they like, and live happy in their teens and twenties.
I'm also passionate about entertaining others with my content: them reacting to it and liking the way I've made it.
:::

If your motivation for making the video is making money through it, it'll be hard to connect with your audience.
==If your motivation is to share your passion and improve other people's lives, you will connect with them.==

sections.title: Passion spreads
sections.md:
- If you're charismatic, you influence others. If you're happy and charismatic, you make others happy too. So a charismatic person who's passionate about something makes others a bit more passionate too. (Studies show it.)
- Positive leaders are more likely to influence an audience than negative leaders, and more likely to persuade followers to do what they want: buy a product, subscribe, eat more grilled cheese.
- The behaviour of leaders changes the happiness and well-being of their followers by influencing their emotional lives.
- It's not that success leads to happiness. **Happiness creates success.**

sections.title: Invite passionate people into your life
sections.md:
> "When you are surrounded with people who share a collective passion around a common purpose, anything is possible."

Use passion as a hiring criterion when you hire people to work on the YouTube channel with you. It's probably the most important one.

> "If it's your passion, then inevitably you'll succeed."

chapters.title: Master the Art of Storytelling
summary: Stories hit emotion first, then logic. Logic alone can't persuade: you need ethos, logos and pathos.
On your channel, pathos is small moments every few seconds. It must be painful not to watch to the end.
Every story has a hero, a villain and townspeople. People want humans, vivid words and someone to root for.

sections.title: Ethos, logos, pathos
sections.md:
Telling a story before you try to make the audience agree with you works, because it hits emotionally first and then logically. "Tell stories to reach people's hearts and minds."

Storytelling is the ultimate tool of persuasion. Brands and people who tell stories (emotional, genuine stories) connect with their audiences in a far deeper, more meaningful way than their competitors.

Aristotle believed persuasive communication happens when three things are present:
- **Ethos:** credibility (achievements, title, experience)
- **Logos:** logic, evidence, data and statistics
- **Pathos:** appealing to emotions

[[fig:persuasion]]

To persuade means influencing someone to act by appealing to reason. But according to some of the most logical minds in the world, ==you simply cannot persuade through logic alone.== You need emotion.

sections.title: Small emotions, every few seconds
sections.md:
On your channel there's a lot of pathos, just not in the usual way. It isn't long emotional stories. It's **small moments every few seconds**:

[[fig:beats]]

- **Curiosity:** "There's one exception…"
- **Surprise:** "I expected this to work, but it didn't."
- **Humour**
- **Suspense:** "We'll come back to this."
- **Relief:** "The good news is…"

sections.title: Break the pattern, open a gap
sections.md:
Personal stories make the brains of the storyteller and the listener sync up: "brain-to-brain coupling". Personal stories with an **unexpected result** are the most compelling (an idea the book takes from Made to Stick).

The most basic way to get someone's attention is to **break a pattern**. Curiosity and mystery grab us. Curiosity happens when we feel a gap in our knowledge. Gaps cause pain: we want to know something but we don't, and to take the pain away we need to fill the gap.

::: key
**It must be painful not to watch the video through to the end.**
:::

When you have a dream in your heart, you know you're going to succeed. Every fail means you're one step closer to winning.

sections.title: People want people
sections.md:
Famous neuroscientists believe we're hardwired for empathy: it's the social glue that holds society together. In a video you create empathy by talking about yourself or about someone else.

> "The truthful, inside story of almost any man's life, if told modestly, is most entertaining. It is almost sure to be good speech material."

==Improving your appearance is not about becoming worthy. It's about removing the barriers that stop you from expressing yourself.==

People like seeing the person who makes the product. That's why KFC has a face, and why you like IcePro and Jawliner. Humans want to see stories of other humans. ==That's why AI-voice YouTube channels can't build a community.==

Every brand and every product has a story. Find it and tell it.

sections.title: What a story is
sections.md:
Jonah Sachs (*Winning the Story Wars*): stories are a kind of communication designed to persuade an audience of the storyteller's worldview. The storyteller puts characters, real or fictional, on a stage and shows what happens to them over time. Each character pursues a goal according to their values, faces difficulty along the way, and succeeds or fails according to the storyteller's view of how the world works.

Audiences today are bombarded with messages, so they're more resistant and sceptical than ever. But when a story inspires them, they spread it for you, and that creates a massive viral effect.

**A hero story** is about one person's success. Your audience wants someone or something to cheer for. They want to be inspired. Give them a hero: yourself, other people, or successful brands.

sections.title: Hero, villain, townspeople
sections.md:
::: blue
Every story has a hero and a villain.
- **The hero** is my product, brand or idea.
- **The villain** is a challenge (like ascending), or the dark side of the community I stand against, or the people who hate the whole idea.
- **The townspeople** are my audience. The hero saves them from the villain, and they live happily ever after.
:::

[[fig:story]]

Give the audience at least one character to root for.

sections.title: Persuade people to join you
sections.md:
To succeed, you have to persuade others to support your vision, dream or cause.

Example, looking for a YouTube team at BUas. Tell a story:

> "You go to university to become a great editor. You come here for 4 years, you pay the university every year, you pay for accommodation and live in this city, and in return you learn a lot about media, and editing is one part of it. But imagine you could work with a successful channel, taught by the editor exactly how to edit, nothing else. These videos get uploaded and you get feedback from real viewers, a lot of them. At some point you edit completely on your own and become a master. You get all of this for free, unlike university. And if you stick with it long enough, you can make a very good amount of money while being part of a cool YouTube team. I'm offering it because I think you're a very cool person and good at editing. Together we can become very successful on YouTube."

Compare that to: *"Hey bro, you know I have a YouTube channel. I really need an editor, but I'm not gonna pay you at all, if that's not a problem. Can you help?"*

sections.title: Vivid words, no clichés
sections.md:
Avoid overused buzzwords and clichés. People hear them all the time, so they've lost their meaning. They get ignored, they're meaningless, and they're boring.

When you describe things people can touch or smell, their sensory cortex activates and they subconsciously feel it. So use metaphors, analogies and vivid language, but no clichés: your audience tunes out phrases they've heard a million times.

**An experiment:** a guy bought cheap objects, wrote a story about each one, and sold them. He spent $127 and sold them for $3,240, because they had stories. Stories raised the value by about 25×.

::: check
It's a real project (Significant Objects). But it's about selling objects, so it doesn't mean a story-video gets 25× the views. "Stories add a lot of value" is the honest version.
:::

chapters.title: Have a Conversation
summary: Practise until delivering the script feels like an exciting conversation with a close friend.
If your voice, gestures and body don't match your words, people stop trusting the message.
Gestures free and natural, an eager style, real feedback, and no fidgeting.

sections.title: The rule: talk like a friend
sections.md:
::: blue
**Practise relentlessly and internalise your content, so you can deliver it as comfortably as having a conversation with a close friend.**
Your note: "Read this again." If you practise the content until you can tell it comfortably, isn't this one of the most important things for your scripts? Yes.
:::

**Why it works:** true persuasion happens after you've built an emotional rapport with your listeners and gained their trust. If your voice, gestures and body language don't match your words, your listeners will distrust your message.

The problem with most technical or scientific presentations is that the presenter fails to make the content visual, interesting and entertaining.

sections.title: Your voice
sections.md:
Get the speed, volume, pauses, emphasis and pitch right for each part of the script. How should you say this next sentence? Is it important? Are you going to let it breathe?

One TED speaker with great pacing (not the fastest, but the best speed for each moment) said he isn't reading to you, he's having a conversation with you. He imagines talking to a friend over dinner in a restaurant.

==In my first video I wasn't speaking in a conversation tone.== That's not how a conversation sounds. It should sound like a conversation, but an **exciting** one: my voice needs to be a lot higher and stronger for the viewer to hear it as normal. Other than that, make it a conversation.

sections.title: Believe what you say
sections.md:
If you don't believe in what you're saying, your body or voice will show it. There's no way to hide it unless you're a trained FBI agent. So believe in your message: don't spread lies, be a firm believer in what you're saying, and show it.

The way you dress, carry yourself and talk is how the audience decides whether to believe you and care. The book says criminals who've shot police officers chose officers who weren't dressed sharp: slouching, bad posture, unconfident. But audiences spot fake confidence too: they've been trained by thousands of videos.

::: check
The police example comes from an FBI interview study with a small number of offenders. Treat it as a story, not proof.
:::

sections.title: Real feedback
sections.md:
Ask many different types of people for real feedback on your video:
1. What did you like most?
2. What did you like least?
3. What did you remember?

The book's three Ps: **Passion, Practice, Presence.**

sections.title: Gestures and body language
sections.md:
Complex thinkers use complex gestures. When somebody is passionate about a topic, he gestures with his hands even if he tries not to.

Pay attention to what your body is saying. Walk, talk and look like a leader people want to follow, in real life too, not just in videos. Learning to command presence (people listen to you, believe you and care about what you say) is charisma and leadership practice. It helps the channel, and it matters when you get people to work with you.

Direct tips from the book:
1. **Use gestures.** Let your hands be free.
2. **Use them sparingly.** Gestures should be natural. Don't think about which to use; your story will guide them.
3. **Use them at key moments.** Save your most expensive gestures for the key moments.
4. **Keep them above the waist.** You want people looking at your eyes, hands and upper body.

Also: stand straight, make eye contact, and wear colours that pop from the background.

sections.title: Eager vs reserved
sections.md:
If you want to make your request or offer more attractive, an **eager** nonverbal style works better.

[[fig:eager]]

- **Eager:** very animated, broad open movements, hands projected outward, leaning forward.
- **Reserved:** leaning back, slower and smaller movements, slower speech.

When you're trying to make a point, cut every mannerism that serves no purpose: playing with a pen, tapping your fingers, spinning around. But move a bit. Don't stay completely still.

sections.title: Before you film
sections.md:
The way you pose changes how you see yourself. Before a speech, if you're alone for 2 minutes, stretch your arms out confidently and take up space: the "power pose".

::: check
The book says it raises testosterone and lowers cortisol. That part failed to replicate (Ranehill 2015). Feeling a bit more confident is the honest claim, so don't put the hormones on camera.
:::

To get your energy up before a speech, jump around, open your body up, and move.

**A staging idea:** one TED speaker with an injury put five chairs next to each other on stage. Each chair was one part of her story: chair 1 the accident, chair 2 the ten days in hospital, and so on. A visual that improves the storytelling.

chapters.title: Teach Me Something New
summary: The brain is wired for novelty: new information, a new package, or a new way to solve an old problem.
Surprise them (the blue/red pattern interrupt) and teach something they can use in daily life.
Know the one big thing, in one sentence that fits in a title. Big picture before details.

sections.title: Why novelty works
sections.md:
Recognising novelty is a hard-wired survival tool all humans share. Our brains look for something brilliant and new, something that stands out, something that looks delicious.

**Teach me something new.** Reveal information that's completely new to your audience, package it differently, or offer a fresh way to solve an old problem.

**Why it works:** the brain loves novelty. An unfamiliar, unusual or unexpected element intrigues the audience, jolts them out of their assumptions, and quickly gives them a new way of looking at the world.

sections.title: Your pattern interrupt
sections.md:
Something I thought of, and it's true:

::: key
Talk about (imaginary) blue and red as if blue is the good one, or let the audience assume blue is healthier. Then ask "so which one should you get?" and answer **"red, because…"**.
The moment you say red, they're shocked. Their mind was careless: they weren't listening deeply because they thought they knew what you'd say. The surprise makes them listen harder, remember the moment and get curious.
:::

sections.title: Teach what they can use
sections.md: The audience wants to learn new things, ideally things they can use in daily life. When I watch Rorz, I want to see something new I should do. That's the only reason I watch: the hope of learning something I can do. ==Teach your audience something they can do that improves their day-to-day life.==

sections.title: The brain's save button
sections.md:
Dopamine gets triggered artificially by gambling and drugs, but a healthy way to get it is learning new information. When something new is rewarding, we tend to remember it, because the brain marks it as important.

How do you use that? Make the information new and exciting. The best teachers keep finding new ways to deliver the same information. Novelty creates enthusiasm in both the teacher and the audience. Get them addicted to learning.

YouTube shows this perfectly: a new type of thumbnail gets you excited and shows information in a new way. When everybody copies it, it stops working, because you've seen it. Then a new type appears and works again.

::: check
Novelty does help memory. "Learning is the best way to get dopamine" is the book's framing, not an established fact.
:::

sections.title: Package it differently
sections.md:
Package your ideas well, especially scientific ones. How can you show it in an interesting visual way? Hans Rosling's moving country bubbles turned boring statistics into a famous talk.

Study successful strategies outside your field: other niches, and other things entirely. If someone speaks persuasively, you can learn from him whether or not he has a YouTube channel.

Old communist buildings repainted in bright colours: same buildings, same people inside, but one looks depressing and the other looks modern and safe. ==Repackage the idea, not just the title and thumbnail.==

Every audience wants a new way to solve its problems. We're wired to look for them.

sections.title: Be a purple cow
sections.md:
We're bombarded with information, and even good stuff gets skipped if it's basic: we've heard it before. Packaged differently, we listen. Have a remarkable style, like Aprilynne Alter: so simple, yet so remarkable.

[[fig:cow]]

If you see a cow on the road you don't care. A purple cow, you're amazed. Only purple cows, you don't care again. **Be remarkable.**

Put your own spin on things. Don't just copy formats. The brain needs something it has never processed to break out of predictable perceptions.

sections.title: Beginner's mind: one big thing
sections.md:
::: key
Can you describe your idea in one sentence? If someone asks a viewer "what was this guy talking about?", he should have one clear answer. One big thing.
Ask: **"What is the one thing I want my audience to know?"** Make sure it fits in a YouTube title.
:::

The audience needs the big picture, then the details. A caveman who meets a tiger doesn't ask how many teeth it has. He asks if it's going to eat him. People need to know **why** before **how**: why we debloat before increasing daily potassium.

chapters.title: Deliver Jaw-Dropping Moments
summary: One shocking, unexpected moment can define a whole talk (Gates' mosquitoes, under 5% of the time).
Emotionally charged events and things that feel important get remembered.
Five ways to create one; end on a showstopper.

sections.title: Bill Gates' mosquitoes
sections.md:
Bill Gates gave a TED talk about malaria. He opened a jar of mosquitoes and said poor people shouldn't be the only ones to experience this. (He later said they weren't infected.) It probably scared some of the crowd, making them feel a little of what people in Africa feel. People reposted it with headlines like "Bill Gates releases swarm of mosquitoes on TED audience".

==It took less than 5% of his talking time, and it's remembered years later.==

Identify the most important points you want to make in the video. Then find a novel, memorable way to deliver them. Sometimes you need to surprise your audience to make them care.

sections.title: Plan the moment first
sections.md:
Before scripting, know what the story is: what makes it interesting, what the format is, and how it's packaged.

Use several senses while planning: seeing, touching, feeling. Stand at a whiteboard, pick up a pen, draw on the laptop, think while walking. Anything that engages more areas of your brain.

Every memorable story, film or presentation has one scene that everyone remembers because it's so impactful.

sections.title: Why it works: emotional events
sections.md:
Psychologists call it an **emotionally charged event**. Gates hooked his audience because it was shocking, unexpected and different, and our brains are wired to remember that kind of moment.

People remember exactly what they were doing when 9/11 happened, who they were with and where, 25 years later. But they don't remember where they left their wallet this morning. One was emotionally charged; the other wasn't.

Emotionally charged = shock, surprise, fear, sadness, joy, wonder.

::: check
The book puts the amygdala in the prefrontal cortex and says it releases dopamine. It's actually in the temporal lobe, and it strengthens memories with stress hormones like noradrenaline. Also, 9/11 memories feel vivid but aren't perfectly accurate. The main point is right: emotional moments get remembered.
:::

sections.title: Importance makes memory
sections.md:
Higher perceived importance gets remembered more. So if someone talks to the YouTuber personally in the Discord, he's far more likely to remember his videos 5 years from now.

I still watch Maurits's videos because I texted with him for one minute, four years ago.

sections.title: 5 ways to create a wow moment
sections.md:
[[fig:wow]]

1. **Props and demos**
2. **Unexpected, shocking statistics**
3. **Pictures, images and videos**
4. **Memorable headlines:** a repeatable line you say. Craft and deliver quotes people repeat.
5. **Personal stories**

sections.title: End on a high note
sections.md:
A showstopper: a mind-blowing moment that seals the deal and brands the message into people's minds. One singer ended her concert by zip-lining across the whole stadium.

So: deliver jaw-dropping moments. It can be a short story, a video, an image, a statistic, something emotional.

chapters.title: Lighten Up
summary: Humour plus novelty is gold. Don't take yourself or your topic too seriously.
Humour lowers defences and makes you likable; funny people get seen as smarter and more stable.
Humorous observations, mostly about yourself, not jokes. Five types. Balance humour, stats and shock.

sections.title: Why humour works
sections.md:
The most popular TED talk ever ("Do schools kill creativity?") has one novel thing about it: humour. We love humour. We love novelty. Combine the two and you've got presentation gold.

**Don't take yourself (or your topic) too seriously.** The brain loves humour. Give your audience something to smile about.

**Why it works:** humour lowers defences. It makes you more likable, and people watch and buy from people they like.

Facts and content on their own are unemotional. You need to package them emotionally, with humour and surprise. Humour is one of the keys to making a message novel.

sections.title: How to use it
sections.md:
Humour is powerful, but you have to use it creatively and naturally. Repeating stupid jokes has the opposite effect. Use it when it actually fits. It's a skill.

::: key
**Make humorous observations instead of telling jokes**: something small, related to what you're talking about.
The humour must not distract from the video. It should **amplify** your words by making people more awake and energised, and so more focused on what you're saying.
:::

==One of the best ways: make the humour about you.== You did something stupid, not your competitor.

sections.title: Humour as a social skill
sections.md:
A good sense of humour is a social skill we admire. Understanding your topic is one thing; having a good sense of humour is another. Combining the two is stronger than relying on one.

- Studies show we attribute other good traits to people with a good sense of humour: friendly, considerate, pleasant, interesting, intelligent, emotionally stable.
- Laughter doesn't just carry information. It spreads positive emotions to others, which makes them more favourable toward the person laughing.
- Humour reduces hostility, deflects criticism, relieves tension, improves morale, and helps communicate difficult messages.

In dating, the book says humour ranks as the most important thing in almost every survey, above career success, education and even physical attraction. That's why you see female superstars dating average funny guys.

::: check
Humour ranks very high in what people *say* they want. But what people say and who they actually choose often differ (speed-dating studies), so don't claim on camera that it beats looks.
:::

sections.title: 5 ways to use humour
sections.md:
1. **Anecdotes and observations:** short stories or examples meant to put a smile on people's faces, not to get a huge laugh.
2. **Analogies and metaphors:** a comparison that shows how two different things are alike. Excellent for explaining complex topics.
3. **Quotes:** funny ones, or ones you comment on in a funny way. Don't grab random famous quotes; do your homework. They can come from anyone, including people you know.
4. **Videos**
5. **Photos**

sections.title: Balance and be yourself
sections.md:
Balance humour, statistics and shock.

Don't take your topic too seriously, and especially don't take yourself seriously. Be authentic and don't try to be something you're not.

==If something made you laugh, there's a big chance it'll make others laugh too.==

chapters.title: Stick to the 18-Minute Rule
summary: About 18 minutes is a good rough length. Heavy thinking tires people, so cut what doesn't need to be there.
Explain it simply. Making things complex is easy; simple takes genius and courage.
Use the rule of 3, and build a message map: one headline, 3 messages, support for each.

sections.title: About 18 minutes
sections.md:
> "You have to be really courageous about your instincts and your ideas. Otherwise you'll just knuckle under, and things that might have been memorable will be lost."

The 18-minute rule is just a good rough timing.

The book says thinking uses glucose, so a lot of thinking makes you physically tired, and that resisting food, watching a presentation and solving a maths puzzle all draw on the same source of energy.

::: check
That "same energy source" idea (ego depletion) failed a big 23-lab replication. The useful part stays true: heavy, dense content tires viewers, so keep it lean.
:::

sections.title: Simple takes courage
sections.md:
> "If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough." (usually credited to Einstein)

::: key
Explaining a complex topic simply is something to strive for every time. People who don't are scared they won't show every little thing they know. When I make a video, the idea isn't to show my audience "look, I know all these complicated things". **It's to inform them in an easy and meaningful way.**
:::

> "Any intelligent fool can make things bigger and more complex. It takes a touch of genius, and a lot of courage, to move in the opposite direction."

That one is usually credited to E. F. Schumacher, though it often gets quoted as Einstein. Either way: courage.

sections.title: The rule of 3
sections.md:
::: key
**Splitting things into 3 always works.** If needed, split each of those 3 into 3 again. Do it as much as possible.
:::

[[fig:rule3]]

It's everywhere:
- My flag has 3 colours.
- You eat with a spoon, knife and fork.
- The US Declaration of Independence has 3 famous rights: life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
- Obama's crowds shouted 3 words: "Yes we can."

It's much easier to take in an idea in 3s.

Another rule-of-3 trick: show 3 things where **the 3rd is the bad one**, or where only the 3rd is good. Don't show them all at once, but one at a time: 1, 2, 3 (surprise). Ryan Trahan does this.

sections.title: The message map
sections.md:
A message map is a very effective communication tool. Use it often. It makes sure your idea is organised.

**Step 1: the headline.** Ask "What is the single most important thing I want my viewer to know about my product, service, brand or idea?" The answer is your headline, e.g. "eat whole foods", "start doing cardio", or "read Atomic Habits and write notes in a notepad". It must be under 140 characters, and shorter is usually better.

**Step 2: support the headline with 3 key messages.** For "eat whole foods": (1) sodium consumption worldwide, (2) the problem with processed foods, (3) what to do instead.

**Step 3: reinforce each message with stories, statistics and examples.** For sodium worldwide: (a) WHO's recommendation vs the world average, (b) what it does to your body, (c) a personal example.

[[fig:message-map]]

The book's example is a message map of Steve Jobs's 2005 Stanford commencement speech, made by the Gallo Communication Group. The speech is built exactly like this: one headline and three stories.

[[fig:jobs-map]]

chapters.title: Paint a Mental Picture with Multisensory Experiences
summary: The brain ignores boring, single-sense content. Pair your words with visuals, especially for beginners.
Paying attention to two things at once is a myth: a simple visual he understands beats a cool edit he can't follow.
Pictures beat words for memory. Mix visual types, balance facts with feeling, and let key numbers stand alone.

sections.title: Touch more than one sense
sections.md:
Deliver presentations with parts that touch more than one sense: sight, sound, touch, taste and smell.

**Why it works:** the brain doesn't pay attention to boring things. Reading plain text, for example, is boring, and it touches only one sense. The brain craves multisensory experiences.

So my videos shouldn't be only verbal, but also visual (images, videos, animations), for a better learning experience.

==Visual + verbal matters most for people with no prior knowledge of the topic.== People who already know it can build the mental model themselves.

sections.title: Multitasking is a myth
sections.md:
::: purple
**When it comes to paying attention, multitasking is a myth.** The brain can't do it well.
So don't try to impress with cool animations. Use simple visual storytelling the viewer can always actually understand.
If you have 2 choices:
1. A really cool edit or visual, but it's a bit too fast and it's hard to focus on what you're saying.
2. Skip the cool edit, and the viewer understands what you're saying.
**Always choose the second.**
:::

[[fig:choice]]

This is biology: we can't pay attention to more than one thing at a time. So what do we do instead? Neuroscience gives us the next idea.

sections.title: Pictures beat words
sections.md:
**The Picture Superiority Effect (PSE):** pictures are superior to words. The book quotes John Medina: "Human PSE is truly Olympian."

[[fig:pse]]

The usual result: when it comes to remembering information later, pictures demolish text and speech. ==Use visuals to enhance your words.==

sections.title: Mix your visuals
sections.md:
::: blue
Charts are good, but chart after chart after chart gets boring. Break the video up with different types of visuals, while still sticking to one specific style. Keep the right balance of both.
:::

When you show statistics, at some point show an individual human with that problem. The viewer's brain gets a break from the charts, and it shows how important the point is. A statistic is data. A picture of the person in the statistic is not just data, it's emotion. You need a balance of facts and emotions.

sections.title: How do you want them to feel?
sections.md:
Don't think only about what you want people to know. **Think about how you want them to feel.**

Today I watched a guy who used to be really ugly and is now very attractive and a model. From what he said, I could tell he knows far more about attractiveness than I do. It gave me a feeling of hope: "yes, I can change, anybody can change how they look." One of the top comments was "anybody can become an 8".

That feeling of hope and security made me remember him better, because now I know I can get even better, and that I can help others improve dramatically, night and day. You get that feeling from seeing someone's before and after.

sections.title: Let one thing stand alone
sections.md:
If I want something highlighted in the viewer's brain, I can show it **on its own for 2 seconds**. If I say "200 people die every month from too much sodium", put a big "200" on screen on a plain background and stay silent for a second. It amplifies the effect, and the viewer actually gets to feel it.

[[fig:alone]]

==That's why intense, fast editing isn't always the answer.==

::: check
The 200 is an example number for the technique, not a real statistic. Use a real, sourced number when you do this in a video.
:::

chapters.title: Stay in Your Lane
summary: Not in your notes yet.
